content: Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) is a severe and potentially life-threatening complication that can arise from an infection with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC). This condition can result in kidney failure, long-term health complications, or even death. It is critical to seek immediate medical attention if any signs of HUS are observed. Signs to Watch For: Individuals with diarrhea who may be developing HUS can exhibit the following symptoms: A significant reduction in urination or complete inability to urinate. A noticeable loss of the pink coloration in the cheeks or the inner lining of the lower eyelids. The appearance of unexplained bruises or small red spots on the skin. The presence of blood in the urine. Extreme fatigue or irritability. A decrease in alertness or awareness. When to Seek Emergency Medical Care: HUS constitutes a medical emergency. If HUS is suspected, it is imperative to contact a healthcare provider or visit the emergency room immediately. Hospitalization is necessary for individuals with HUS, as their kidneys may cease functioning, and they may develop other severe complications. While most patients recover within a few weeks, some may experience permanent health issues or succumb to the condition. Who is at Risk for HUS: Although anyone can develop HUS, it is most commonly observed in children under the age of five who have diarrhea. Causes of HUS: The primary cause of HUS is an infection with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC), which accounts for approximately 80% of HUS cases in children. Other causes include: Infections with other pathogens that cause diarrhea, vomiting, or gastrointestinal symptoms. Pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae bacteria. Certain medications, such as some chemotherapy drugs. Types of HUS: HUS can be categorized into two forms: typical and atypical. Typical HUS is associated with diarrhea and is most often linked to STEC infections. Atypical HUS encompasses all other forms of the condition, which are frequently caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors. Atypical HUS can lead to chronic or recurrent symptoms and may result in more severe health complications, such as persistent high blood pressure, kidney failure, and widespread blood clot formation throughout the body.
